Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset: a purple-to-orange sky, a pale sun low over a purple hill on the left, a gold sun path on the water, and the boat's broken reflection

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

16 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the sailboat, right of center Light: the low setting sun just above the horizon, a little left of center, behind the scene; the sun path and the sails' left sides catch itHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: Paint the purple hillFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch flat: Add the bright gold dashesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Add the light deck railLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #2 round: Zigzag the mast's reflectionRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The sails; 2 The red hull. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 3.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 4.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 7.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 9.
  • Liner work, first in step 11. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Pull-down, first in step 13.
  • Zigzag, first in step 16.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sunset sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 16 · The sunset sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Twilight violet, Sunset pink, then Sunset orange.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: The light comes from the low sun just above the horizon, a little left of center, so the sky is brightest orange there and darkest violet at the top. Run the orange all the way down past the horizon, a bit over halfway down the canvas, so no white shows under the hill and sea. Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 16 · The sunset sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 6 in from the left edge; it's about 1 in wide and 1 in tall.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Move the tip of the brush in small circles, working outward from the middle of the sun to its round edge.
  7. It should leave a round disk with a soft edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with a few lighter circular passes.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is about 1 in across, centered about 6 3/4 in from the left edge, and its bottom almost touches the hill's long slope. Yellow is see-through, so if the orange shows through, let it dry and give it a second coat.

Then. Smooth with the same circular motion, and highlight only the lit top edges.

Little circles along the top

If it goes wrong.

  • The edge is too hard. Soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.

The far hill and shore 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 16 · The far hill and shore, 1 of 2

Paint the purple hill

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 6 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Hill purple.
  5. Mix enough Hill purple for this step and step 4; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Bend every stroke with the shape: over the hill's rounded top, then down along its long slope to the right.
  8. It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes the hill look sloped.

Tip: The hill's rounded top is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge, and its long slope runs down to the right until it meets the horizon just left of the sun. Paint it right over the orange sky.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

STEP 4 OF 16 · The far hill and shore, 2 of 2

Paint the far shoreline

  1. Let the purple hill and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 13 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  3. Paint: Hill purple.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave a flat, level band that reads as distant land, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
  7. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: It's a level band about 1/2 in tall, a bit over halfway down the canvas, running right across under the hill and behind where the boat will go. Keep its top edge straight and level.

The sea 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 16 · The sea, 1 of 2

Lay in the deep teal sea

  1. Let the far hill and shore, and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 1/2 in from the top edge.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave flat, level bands that read as water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: Paint straight over where the sun path and the boat's reflection will go; they go on top later. Keep every stroke level, right up to the bottom of the shoreline.

STEP 6 OF 16 · The sea, 2 of 2

Add the lighter sea streaks

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Muted sea green.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave level streaks of lighter color with the darker sea between them, like gentle ripples.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Lay the streaks thinner and closer together near the horizon and longer and wider apart toward the bottom. Leave plenty of the darker sea from step 5 showing between them. This is the ugly stage for many painters, and that's normal: it comes together once the gold and the boat go on. The few warm flecks scattered across the sea in the picture go on with the sun path's dashes in steps 7 and 8. You can skip streaks in the patch below where the boat will go; its reflection covers it.

The sun path 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 16 · The sun path, 1 of 2

Lay the dusky gold path

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 10 in wide and 4 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dusky gold.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  5. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  6. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the water color between them.
  7. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.

Tip: The path is a column of dashes straight below the sun, narrow at the horizon and widening toward the bottom of the canvas, with a few stray dashes off to the left. Let the sea dry first so the dashes stay crisp. Near the horizon the dashes sit so close they almost join into one band; lower down, leave teal gaps between them.

The sailboat 4 steps

STEP 9 OF 16 · The sailboat, 1 of 4

Paint the two sails

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 1/4 in from the right edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Warm sail white.
  5. Mix enough Warm sail white for this step and steps 11 and 14; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape: the big left triangle. Then add the narrower right triangle beside it, touching it. The mast goes on top later.
  8. It should leave two clean triangles side by side, reading as one white sail shape.

Tip: The left sail is the bigger triangle; its point is about 3 in from the top edge and about 11 1/4 in from the left edge, and its bottom sits a little over halfway down. The right sail is a narrower triangle beside it. The sun is on the left, so the left edges of the sails catch the most light.

Stroke: Building from pieces how to do it, not checked yet

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the picture shows smooth ribs; otherwise leave the segments visible.

STEP 10 OF 16 · The sailboat, 2 of 4

Paint the red hull

  1. Let the sails and the sea dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 1 in tall.
  5. Paint: Hull red.
  6. Mix enough Hull red for this step and step 15; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Start with one simple shape, a long low rectangle. Then round each end with a short curved piece, like ( ), so the hull narrows to the waterline.
  9. It should leave a long red shape with curved ends, wider at the top than at the waterline.

Tip: The hull is about 3 in long and a little under 1/2 in tall, wider at the top than the bottom, with its bottom edge sitting on the water. It overlaps the bottom of the sails slightly.

STEP 11 OF 16 · The sailboat, 3 of 4

Add the light deck rail

  1. Let the red hull and the sails dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Warm sail white.
  5. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure, and pull one thin line along the top edge of the hull. A little wobble is fine.
  7. It should leave a thin, flowing line.
  8. Leave what step 10 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  9. Warm sail white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  10. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: Pull the line along the very top of the red, from one end of the hull to the other. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset: a purple-to-orange sky, a pale sun low over a purple hill on the left, a golden sun path on the water, and the boat's broken reflection.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is a painted scene edge to edge, with no bars, text, border, or frame around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (an 11x14 canvas on its side)

Done: crop

Left out: about 15% of the width: a strip of the hill's left end and of open water and sky at the right edge

Why: fit-canvas picked a crop: the 3:2 photo is wider than the 14:11 canvas, and cropping about 7.5% from each side keeps the sun, its path, the boat and its reflection whole at no cost.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: none besides the boat, which is the subject. Textures of hundreds of items: no, the water and sun path are one repeated mark (level horizontal dashes). Detail inside big shapes: no, the sky is loose horizontal strokes. Parts: about 8 (sky, sun, hill, far shore, water, sun path, boat, reflection), within detail_budget.max_parts 8 for a 154 sq in canvas.

Why: Every answer is no; the picture is already a loose painted scene at beginner level, so the lesson is made from the fitted photo.

A simple, bold sunset seascape: bands of sky, a dark far hill and shore, teal water with a gold sun path, and one small red sailboat with a broken reflection as the focal point. What's hard for a beginner is keeping the sky blend smooth across three colors, keeping the dashes level and sized by distance, and making the reflection softer than the boat. The lesson is about painting back to front and building water in layers.

Subject: A small red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset: a purple-to-orange sky, a pale sun low over a purple hill on the left, a gold sun path on the water, and the boat's broken reflection
Focal point: the sailboat, right of center
Light: the low setting sun just above the horizon, a little left of center, behind the scene; the sun path and the sails' left sides catch it

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. Purple hill
  3. Far shoreline
  4. The sea
  5. The sails
  6. The red hull
  7. Mast and boom
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

The owner's chosen beginner approach for acrylic (docs/decisions.md): white canvas, sky first, back to front, one brush move per step. The scene is a sunset sky, a far hill, water with a sun path, and one sailboat with a reflection, which paint-along tutorials teach exactly this way, and the technique has the water-reflection rules this picture needs.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

Starts from a toned ground with a separate flat block-in; the owner picked paint-along for acrylic beginners, and this picture is already simple flat bands that paint-along covers.

How the paint recipes were worked out14 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Twilight violet Delta E 4.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part red

  • Sunset pink Delta E 2.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts red, 3 parts white, 1 part ultramarine

  • Sunset orange Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

  • Pale sun yellow Delta E 2.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 2 parts yellow, 1 part red

  • Hill purple Delta E 1.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow

  • Deep teal Delta E 6.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

  • Muted sea green Delta E 3.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts white, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part yellow

  • Dusky gold Delta E 2.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts white, a touch of yellow

  • Bright gold Delta E 1.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part yellow, 1 part red, 1 part white, a touch of ultramarine

  • Warm sail white Delta E 2.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

  • Hull red Delta E 3.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of white

  • Mast brown Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part white

  • Reflection gray Delta E 4.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow

  • Soft blue-gray Delta E 3.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna

Furthest off: Delta E 6.1. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order16 steps

Back to front, as the technique says: the sky first, blended wet and run past the horizon, then the sun on it; the hill and the far shore over the sky; the sea over its bottom edge; the sun path on the dry sea; the boat (sails, hull, rail, mast) over the sea; and the reflection last, after everything above the water is dry, as the research's water-reflection order says.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The farthest thing, one wet blend from violet to orange, run past the horizon so the hill and sea go over it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Sits on the sky, so it goes on once the sky is dry; it sets the light for the whole picture.

  3. 3. Paint the purple hill

    The next farthest thing, painted over the dry sky.

  4. 4. Paint the far shoreline

    A dark band at the horizon in front of the hill, with the same paint while it's mixed.

  5. 5. Lay in the deep teal sea

    The water's base coat in its darkest main color, over the shore's bottom edge.

  6. 6. Add the lighter sea streaks

    Lighter ripple streaks over the dry base, the second value of the water.

  7. 7. Lay the dusky gold path

    The sun path's darker dashes first, on dry water, so the bright ones can sit on them.

  8. 8. Add the bright gold dashes

    The brightest dashes last in the path, in the middle where the light is strongest.

  9. 9. Paint the two sails

    The boat sits in front of the sea; its biggest, lightest piece goes first.

  10. 10. Paint the red hull

    The hull below the sails, one flat red.

  11. 11. Add the light deck rail

    A light line on the dry hull, a small value change after its base.

  12. 12. Line in the mast and boom

    The thin dark line over the dry sails, last on the boat.

  13. 13. Pull down the soft gray reflection

    The reflection goes on after everything above the water is dry: its soft base first.

  14. 14. Pull down the light of the sails

    The sails' light pulled down into the reflection, a little darker than the sails.

  15. 15. Pull down the red of the hull

    The hull's red pulled down right under it.

  16. 16. Zigzag the mast's reflection

    The mast's zigzag reflection, the last and thinnest mark.

A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Text check: missing Step 4: The shoreline right of the boat (the last inch at the right edge) isn't in this step's outline; it was painted with the sky in step 1, so the shore band looks short on the right until then. (left: the outline tool gave the strip right of the boat to the sky)

  • Text check: flat Step 13: The reflection has ragged ripple edges and level teal gaps; the text gave only straight-down strokes. (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The OpenAI SDK refuses to start without an API key even though the proxy injects one; renders ran with a placeholder OPENAI_API_KEY in the command's environment.
  • outline: the far shoreline right of the boat (frame x 0.84-1) stays with the sky. points_in there, then two boxes for the shore, didn't take it; the boat splits the band and the small right piece goes to the sky. It's dark in the sky's blend, so it reads fine, but the shore step doesn't paint it.
  • Kuwahara simplify wipes out the mast at strength 2 and 3; meanshift kept it.
  • paints --add sails found no second sail color (Delta E 5.5), so the sails are one full step, not dark/mid/light.
  • Rewrote drafted card lines for this subject: small-circles (clouds -> the sun disk), curved-strokes (pumpkin/balloon -> the hill), horizontal-strokes result (ground -> distant land and water), build-from-pieces (oval and ( ) -> two triangles for the sails, a rectangle with curved ends for the hull), liner ('for branches' -> the deck rail and mast), pull-down result ('a tree, boat, or shore' -> the boat), zigzag (post or plank -> the mast).
  • The cards horizontal-strokes, curved-strokes, build-from-pieces and small-circles have no load line, and several have no mistakes line (check notes).
  • No card for the dark line under a hull at the waterline; it's added as a tip on the zigzag step with the same gray.
  • The text review was done in the same context (no Agent tool in this run).

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 4, Paint the far shoreline: The shoreline right of the boat (the last inch at the right edge) isn't in this step's outline; it was painted with the sky in step 1, so the shore band looks short on the right until then.
  • The text review was done by the same session that wrote the text, not a fresh one.
